outcomes.text: Define social order and social control, and compare how functionalism, Marxism, Weberians, feminism, the New Right, pluralism and postmodernism view them.
Define social change and compare the theoretical views of how society changes over time.
Define conflict and consensus and compare how each perspective treats them.
Distinguish social structure from social action and place each theory on that divide.
Explain the role of values in society and how each perspective sees them.
Explain the two-way link between sociology and social policy, and each perspective's view of policy.

topics.title: Theme 1: Introducing socialisation, culture and identity

outcomes.text: Define culture, norms and values and explain their relative nature across time, culture and society.
Distinguish subculture, high culture, popular culture, global culture and consumer culture, with their norms and values.
Explain cultural diversity and cultural hybridity, including code switching.
Define primary and secondary socialisation.
Explain how the family, peer group, media, religion, education and workplace socialise individuals.
Use conflict, consensus and social action theory to explain how agencies socialise people into norms and values.
Explain formal agencies of social control: the criminal justice system and government.
Explain informal agencies of social control: family, peers, media, religion, education and workplace.
Explain the overlap between formal and informal social control in work, education and religion.
Describe identities based on ethnicity and nationality, with their cultural characteristics and values.
Describe identities based on gender, social class and sexuality.
Describe identities based on age and disability, including the medical and social models.
Explain how identities are created through agencies of socialisation.
Explain hybrid identities and how identity can be fluid.
Explain how identity changes socially over time.
Describe the diversity of UK family and household types, including nuclear, extended, lone parent, reconstituted, same-sex, non-family and lone-person households.
Explain changing sociological understanding of family life, including trends in marriage, divorce and cohabitation.
Explain demographic changes and their reasons: birth rate, family size, age at marriage and childbearing, and ageing population.
Explain the functionalist view of the family, including the universal family and 'warm bath' theory.
Explain the New Right view of the nuclear family, traditional marriage and gender roles.
Explain Marxist views of the family, capitalism and reproduction of the labour force.
Explain feminist views of the family: Marxist, liberal, radical and post-feminism.
Explain the postmodernist view: individualisation, confluent love and choice.

subtopics.title: Roles and relationships in the family

outcomes.text: Explain the domestic division of labour, paid work, symmetrical family and joint conjugal roles.
Explain emotional work, the triple shift, childcare and caring for elderly relatives.
Explain finances, decision making, power and control, including lagged adaptation and coercive control.
Explain the 'dark side' of the family, including domestic abuse and neglect.

subtopics.title: Children and childhood in the family

outcomes.text: Explain the role of children, friends and extended family.
Explain the growth of child-centred families.
Explain the extension of childhood and toxic childhood.
Explain functionalist views of youth culture: transitional stage and social integration.
Explain Marxist and neo-Marxist views: spectacular subcultures, resistance and magical solutions.
Explain feminist views, including bedroom culture and malestream sociology.
Explain postmodernist views: neo-tribes and supermarket of style.
Explain subcultural norms and values linked to social class, including resistance and bricolage.
Explain subcultural norms and values linked to gender and ethnicity.
Explain hybridity and cultural appropriation in subcultures.
Describe online, criminal, anti-school, urban music and female deviant subcultures.
Explain the role of norms and values in these subcultures and their threat to social order.
Describe patterns and trends in youth deviance by class, gender, ethnicity and location, using sociological research and official statistics.
Explain participation in deviant subcultures using functionalist strain theory and subcultural theories.
Explain participation using New Right, Marxist and neo-Marxist views.
Explain participation using interactionist labelling and feminist views.
Explain the media's role in deviancy amplification, moral panics and folk devils.
Explain identity-based explanations involving ethnicity, gender and class.
Evaluate evidence on how ethnicity, gender and sexuality are represented, and how this is changing.
Evaluate evidence on how social class and age are represented in the media.
Explain how social groups intersect in media representation.
Explain Marxist and neo-Marxist views: ruling-class hegemony and power inequalities.
Explain pluralist views: supply and demand, diversity, choice and the Fourth Estate.
Explain feminist views: the male gaze and beauty myth.
Explain postmodernist views: saturation, globalisation and hyper-reality.
Explain direct models of media effects such as the hypodermic syringe.
Explain indirect models: the cultural effects and two-step flow models.
Explain active audience models: uses and gratifications and reception theory.
Explain the media as an agency of social control affecting social order.
Explain the media's role in deviancy amplification, labelling, moral panics and folk devils.
Describe patterns and trends in media consumption by class, gender, ethnicity and age, and the influence on identity and values.

units.title: Component 02: Researching and understanding social inequalities

topics.title: Theme 3 Section A: Research methods and researching social inequalities

outcomes.text: Explain positivism: patterns, trends, objectivity, value freedom, generalisation and quantitative data.
Explain interpretivism: meanings, Verstehen, rapport, subjectivity, bias, reflexivity and qualitative data.
Evaluate research using validity, reliability, representativeness and generalisability.
Explain factors influencing the choice of topic and methods, including funding and the funding body.
Explain aims, hypotheses, research questions, primary and secondary data, operationalisation, pilot studies, data collection and interpretation.
Explain random sampling: random, systematic and stratified.
Explain non-random sampling: snowball, volunteer, opportunity and quota.
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each sampling technique.
Explain access and gatekeeping, and ethical considerations such as British Sociological Association principles.
Explain how sociological research contributes to contemporary social policy.
Evaluate questionnaires and structured interviews.
Evaluate official and non-official statistical data and content analysis.
Evaluate participant, non-participant, covert and overt observation.
Evaluate unstructured and semi-structured interviews.
Distinguish quantitative from qualitative data, and explain ethnographic methods and longitudinal studies.
Explain mixed methods: triangulation and methodological pluralism.

topics.title: Theme 3 Section B: Understanding social inequalities

outcomes.text: Describe evidence of inequality by social class, including social mobility and social closure.
Describe evidence of inequality by gender: segregation, pay gap and glass ceiling.
Describe evidence of inequality by ethnicity: concrete ceiling, institutional racism and under-representation.
Explain inequalities in work, employment, health and poverty and their effect on life chances.
Explain inequality using functionalist meritocracy and value consensus, and Marxist class conflict, alienation and ideology.
Explain inequality using feminist dual burden and patriarchy, and Weberian status, party and class.
Explain how social policies on class, gender and ethnicity aim to reduce inequality.

topics.title: Theme 4: Globalisation and the digital social world

outcomes.text: Define globalisation and discuss problems with the definition.
Describe the digital revolution, global village, virtual communities, networked society and social media.
Explain how digital communication links to social capital and access.
Apply Marxist and neo-Marxist ideas of ownership, control and ideology to digital communication.
Apply feminist ideas: patriarchy, exploitation and fourth-wave feminism.
Apply postmodernist ideas: diversity, identity and hyper-reality.
Explain the impact on identity, relationships and values by social class, gender and age.
Explain the impact on inequalities by class, gender, age and location, including regulation and censorship.
Explain the digital divide by income and location.

subtopics.title: Global social change and the digital world

outcomes.text: Explain the impact on social order, conflict and change, including religious fundamentalism.
Explain cultural homogenisation: westernisation, capitalism and consumerism.
Explain cultural defence and glocalisation, including reverse colonisation and indigenous cultures.
Define crime, deviance, social control and social order.
Explain the relativity and social construction of crime and deviance.
Evaluate official crime statistics, victim surveys and self-report studies.
Describe the social distribution of offending and victimisation by class, gender, age and ethnicity.
Describe global organised crime.
Describe green crime, primary and secondary.
Explain how transnational criminal groups use countries in the global south.
Explain crime using functionalism: anomie, strain and safety valve.
Explain crime using subcultural theories: status frustration, focal concerns and illegitimate opportunity structures.
Explain crime using Marxism: repressive state apparatus, alienation and capitalist ideology.
Explain crime using interactionism: master status, self-fulfilling prophecy and subterranean values.
Explain crime using left and right realism, and feminism.
Explain social and community crime prevention, including multi-agency working and consensual policing.
Explain situational and environmental crime prevention: target hardening, displacement, zero tolerance and broken windows.
Explain restorative justice, rehabilitation and retributive justice.
Explain surveillance, greater equality policies, and the effectiveness of policies in maintaining social order.
Explain functionalist, Marxist, liberal, social democratic, New Right and feminist views of education's role.
Explain the relationship between education and work, including role allocation, correspondence principle, hidden curriculum and vocationalism.
Describe patterns and trends in attainment by class, ethnicity and gender.
Describe educational provision around the world, including gender apartheid and education poverty.
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of measuring educational attainment.
Explain differential attainment by inside-school factors such as the ethnocentric curriculum and streaming.
Explain differential attainment by outside-school, material and cultural factors, including cultural capital.
Apply functionalist, Marxist, interactionist, social democratic, feminist and New Right views.
Explain how class, gender and ethnicity intersect in attainment.

subtopics.title: Changes in the UK education system

outcomes.text: Describe the diversity of educational institutions: academies, independent schools and free schools.
Explain government policies from the 1988 Education Reform Act, including vocational training and the pupil premium.
Explain New Right and social democratic influences on policy.
Assess policy impact on inclusion, access, competition, choice and standards, and on gender, class and ethnicity.

topics.title: Theme 5, Option 3: Religion, belief and faith

outcomes.text: Define religion, faith and belief.
Distinguish churches, denominations, sects, cults, new religious movements, new age movements and fundamentalism.
Explain measures of religion: belief, participation, religiosity and belief without belonging.
Discuss the complexity and issues of measuring religion.
Describe patterns of religion by class, gender, ethnicity, age and location, and why religions appeal to different groups.
Explain the global significance of religion, differences between societies, and links to industrialisation, migration and technology.
Explain the resurgence and decline of religion.
Explain functionalist views: social solidarity, rituals and collective conscience.
Explain Marxist and neo-Marxist views: false consciousness and religion as a conservative force.
Explain Weberian views on social change and the Protestant work ethic.
Explain feminist and postmodernist views of religion.
Explain the growth of fundamentalist groups and how they challenge traditional theories.
Debate secularisation in belief, practice, fundamentalism and religious influence.
Explain pro-secularisation theories: rationalisation and societalisation.
Explain anti-secularisation theories: postmodern views and spiritual growth.
Explain UK government policy on religious equality, discrimination and freedom.
